overview: Two classic mechanisms by which an inhibitor reduces enzyme activity, distinguished by where the inhibitor binds and how kinetics change.
genZNote: Competitive fights for the active site. Noncompetitive just changes the vibe.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: An inhibitor that structurally resembles the substrate and binds the enzyme's active site, blocking substrate binding.
aspects.valueB: An inhibitor that binds a site other than the active site (allosteric site), changing the enzyme's shape and reducing catalytic efficiency.

aspects.label: Binding Site
aspects.valueA: Active site — directly competes with substrate.
aspects.valueB: Allosteric site, distinct from the active site.

aspects.label: Effect on Vmax
aspects.valueA: Vmax unchanged — enough substrate can outcompete the inhibitor.
aspects.valueB: Vmax decreased — inhibitor reduces functional enzyme regardless of substrate concentration.

aspects.label: Effect on Km
aspects.valueA: Apparent Km increased — more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity.
aspects.valueB: Km unchanged — substrate still binds normally, just less productively.

aspects.label: Reversibility With Substrate
aspects.valueA: Can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.
aspects.valueB: Cannot be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.

aspects.label: Classic Example
aspects.valueA: Malonate inhibiting succinate dehydrogenase; methotrexate on dihydrofolate reductase.
aspects.valueB: Cyanide inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase at a non-substrate site.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Increases Km, Vmax unchanged, overcome by excess substrate.
aspects.valueB: Decreases Vmax, Km unchanged, not overcome by excess substrate.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Lineweaver-Burk plots: competitive inhibitors share the same y-intercept (1/Vmax); noncompetitive inhibitors share the same x-intercept (-1/Km).
overlay.memoryTrick: "Competitive: more substrate wins. Noncompetitive: more substrate doesn't matter."
